pathway.title: TRANSALTA CORP — Credit Snapshot
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: First, leverage is above management's target and has moved the wrong way for a reason that is earnings, not debt: the financial base handoff shows Total Consolidated Net Debt down from 3,725 to 3,450 and credit facility drawings repaid from 95 to nil, yet last-four-quarter Adjusted EBITDA fell from 1,104 to 1,006, lifting the reported ratio from 4.0 times to 4.1 times. The fall in nine-month Adjusted EBITDA (759 against 857) is more than explained by Energy Transition (down 90, the end of coal at Centralia) and Hydro (down 48, lower Alberta prices and credit sales), while Gas improved by 32 and the third quarter was up 26. The Centralia loss is permanent in the sources' terms; the Hydro fall depends on Alberta prices. Creditors should read the 4.1 times as a ratio whose denominator has not yet stabilised.

Second, liquidity and near-term maturities are comfortable on reported figures: 1,867 of Available liquidity against long-term debt maturing of 550 across 2026 to 2028 (calculated below, about 3.39 times), no cash drawings, and facility extensions to 2030 and 2028. Two qualifications apply: 211 of non-committed letters of credit reduce committed availability, and some cash is held in project entities (the sources give 100 and 84 for restricted cash and do not reconcile them), so the freely movable share of the 345 of cash is not calculable.

Third, the cash generation base is weaker than the earnings headline suggests. Operating cash flow was 317 against 415, free cash flow 338 against 421, and the nine-month cash increase of 140 would have been a decrease of 198 without 338 of share proceeds, which were raised mainly to pre-fund the Colorado cash price. Free cash flow still covered common dividends of 59 with 279 to spare, so distributions are not the pressure point; acquisitions, debt repayment and the Centralia Order costs are.

Fourth, the October 2026 transactions shift the debt profile in ways the Sept. 30 statements do not show. The Colorado acquisition adds US$750 million of assumed project debt and contracted peaking capacity of 318 MW; the Oklahoma sale brings in US$305 million of cash and gives an outside investor 49 per cent of that wind portfolio. The sources supply neither the acquired earnings nor the debt terms, so the direction of net leverage cannot be determined from the pack.

Fifth, the Centralia Order imposes costs that are real cash costs and excluded from Adjusted EBITDA (38 over nine months, 27 in Q3). The unit's coal-fired operations ended but a federal order keeps it available in 90-day steps, and FERC rejected the first two cost recovery petitions while allowing new ones. If the Order continues without recovery, deducting the nine-month cost lifts the illustrative leverage figures to 4.36 times total debt and 4.00 times net debt (financial base handoff, Calculations C10, which excludes any pre-2026 Order cost).

runs.text: Strengths. Liquidity: 1,867 of Available liquidity, no cash drawn on 2,222 of committed facilities, extended maturities, and small debt maturities in 2026 (52) and 2027 (332). Revenue visibility: 53 per cent of capacity is contracted with a weighted average life of 9 years, and hedged production is 9,364 GWh for 2026 and 6,732 GWh for 2027, which the sources show absorbed most of the 2026 fall in Alberta spot prices (realized merchant price 104 against 107 while spot fell to 32 from 44). Diversification: 89 facilities in four regions across hydro, wind and solar and gas. Balance sheet repair in absolute terms: drawn credit facilities repaid, Total Consolidated Net Debt down by 275, interest expense down to 241 from 266 over nine months. Contracted growth: Far North and Colorado add contracted gas capacity, and the Centralia conversion has a tolling agreement with capacity payments through 2044. Prudent pre-funding: the Colorado cash price was equity funded before closing.

Weaknesses. Leverage above target at 4.1 times with the calculated total and net ratios at 4.19 and 3.85 times, and rising since December. Narrowed earnings base: nine-month Adjusted EBITDA down 98, with a lost coal earnings stream and unquantified effects from the mothballed thermal units (Sheerness Unit 1, Battle River Units 4 and 5, Sundance 6). Alberta concentration: 61 per cent of capacity and 77 per cent merchant exposure, with hedge cover that the sources document only to 2027. Structural opacity: 1,585 of non-recourse and OCP debt behind distribution tests (one entity failed its test), exchangeable securities of 750 classified as current, US$750 million of assumed project debt, and no guarantee or ranking detail for 1,673 of senior unsecured debt. Cash flow softness: operating cash flow 317 against 415 and free cash flow 338 against 421, and a nine-month cash build dependent on share proceeds. Unrecovered Order costs and a negative outlook at one rating agency, with up to 59 of credit-contingent collateral. Reliance on management-defined measures for EBITDA, net debt and free cash flow, none of which can be tied to covenant definitions from the pack.

blocks.title: Transaction summary and new debt issues

runs.text: Colorado acquisition (subsequent event, closed Oct. 22, 2026). The company acquired Mountain Peak Power and Canyon Peak Power, two fully contracted natural gas-fired peaking facilities totalling 318 MW near Denver, from an indirect subsidiary of Blackstone, Inc. The purchase price was US$1 billion, including the assumption of US$750 million of project debt; the US$250 million cash portion was funded by the common share offering completed on June 9, 2026 (18,230,000 shares at 19.20 per share, gross proceeds of about 350). The agreement was announced on June 3, 2026 and was subject to Canyon Peak Power reaching commercial in-service and regulatory approvals; closing came on Oct. 22, 2026 (Q2 release page:4 and page:5; Q3 release page:5 and page:98). The accounting is a business combination whose fair values and purchase price allocation are not yet determined (Q3 release page:98). Credit mechanism: the group takes on US$750 million of project-level debt that is not on the Sept. 30 balance sheet, backed by contracted peaking assets, while the cash cost was pre-funded with equity. The sources give no EBITDA, debt terms, amortization or covenants for the assumed project debt, so its effect on consolidated leverage is not calculable and its ranking against group creditors is Insufficient Information.

Oklahoma wind minority sale (subsequent event, completed Oct. 22, 2026). The company sold a 49 per cent interest in its 500 MW Oklahoma wind portfolio (White Rock West, White Rock East, Horizon Hill) to Ares Infrastructure funds for cash proceeds of US$305 million before closing adjustments, and keeps operational oversight under a long-term asset management agreement (Q3 release page:5, page:98). Credit mechanism: cash comes in and the company keeps control and an operating role, but a co-owner now takes 49 per cent of the portfolio's cash flows, giving an outside investor 49 per cent of the portfolio; the accounting treatment, the EBITDA given up and the use of proceeds are not supplied. Management describes the transaction as "strengthening our balance sheet" (Management Language, Q3 release page:2); that effect is not quantified in the pack.

Far North (closed Feb. 2, 2026). Four natural gas-fired facilities totalling 310 MW in Ontario for a purchase price of 95 subject to adjustments (aggregate 107 including working capital adjustments of 12), funded from cash and credit facility borrowings (Q1 release page:4; Q3 release page:77). The acquired business contributed revenue of 27 and earnings before taxes of 4 from Feb. 2 to Sept. 30, 2026 (Q3 release page:77).

Share offering (June 9, 2026). 18,230,000 common shares at 19.20 for gross proceeds of about 350; proceeds were pre-funding for the Colorado cash price and were partly used meanwhile to repay drawings on the syndicated credit facility (Q2 release page:5). Net proceeds of 338 are in the nine-month cash flow statement (Q3 release page:70).

Credit facility extension (July 17, 2026). The syndicated facility moved from June 30, 2029 to June 30, 2030 and the bilateral facilities from June 30, 2027 to June 30, 2028 (Q3 release page:40). This is a maturity extension of existing committed facilities, not new money.

New debt issues. No new note, bond or term loan issue is reported for 2026 in the sources; the only debt issuance in the cash flow statements is 450 in the nine months ended Sept. 30, 2025, with none in 2026 (Q3 release page:70), and the company says 2025 refinancings lowered interest cost on certain senior notes (Q3 release page:19). The terms of the 2025 notes are not supplied. The US$750 million of project debt becomes consolidated through the Colorado acquisition but is assumed, not issued by the company.

Mothballing and wind-down of coal. Centralia Unit 2 ceased coal-fired operations at the end of 2025 and remains available for operation under successive 90-day U.S. Department of Energy orders, the latest running to Dec. 12, 2026; costs to comply are recorded in operating expense and excluded from Adjusted EBITDA; FERC rejected two cost recovery petitions on Oct. 1 and 19, 2026 with new petitions allowed (Q3 release page:32, page:65). The coal-to-gas conversion is supported by a tolling agreement with Puget Sound Energy through 2044 (Q3 release page:44).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: TransAlta enters the cutoff with ample liquidity but a weaker earnings base than a year ago. On management's own measure, Adjusted Net Debt to Adjusted EBITDA was 4.1 times at Sept. 30, 2026 against 4.0 times at Dec. 31, 2025, so the ratio now sits above the stated long-term target range of 3.0 to 4.0 times. The rise came from the denominator: last-four-quarter Adjusted EBITDA fell from 1,104 to 1,006 while Adjusted Net Debt fell from 4,396 to 4,121. On a plain balance-sheet basis that treats the 750 of exchangeable securities as debt, the calculated ratios are 4.19 times gross and 3.85 times net of unrestricted cash at Sept. 30, 2026. Liquidity is strong in the sources' own terms: 1,867 of available liquidity, no cash drawn on the 2,222 of committed facilities, and the syndicated facility extended to June 2030 and the bilateral facilities to June 2028 on July 17, 2026. Scheduled debt maturities are small relative to liquidity, with 52 due in 2026 and 332 in 2027 on the maturity table, but a large share of the debt is project-level and subject to distribution tests, so group liquidity is not all freely movable. The earnings picture is mixed: the third quarter improved (Adjusted EBITDA 264 against 238) on stronger Gas and Energy Marketing results, but nine-month Adjusted EBITDA is 759 against 857, because Centralia Unit 2 ceased coal-fired operations at the end of 2025 and Alberta spot prices fell. Cash flow from operations also fell, and the nine-month cash increase relied on 338 of common share proceeds. Events after quarter end (the US$1 billion Colorado acquisition with US$750 million of assumed project debt, the US$305 million sale of a 49 per cent interest in the Oklahoma wind portfolio, and the mothballing of Battle River Units 4 and 5 and Sundance 6) change the capital structure in ways the Sept. 30 statements do not show. No figure here comes from audited FY2025 statements: FY2025 comparatives are limited to the Dec. 31, 2025 balance sheet, management-reported full-year measures and the quarterly table.

fields.value: The source states that nine-month Adjusted EBITDA fell by 98, or 11 per cent, and that the third quarter rose by 26 (Q3 release page:22). The segment table shows where: Energy Transition fell by 90 over nine months (84 to (6)) and Hydro by 48 (246 to 198), while Gas rose by 32 and Corporate improved by 14 (Calculations C8). The source attributes the Energy Transition fall to no production at Centralia Unit 2 after it ceased coal-fired operations at the end of 2025 (page:18, page:32), so this is a lost earnings stream, not a timing effect. Hydro fell on lower Alberta spot and ancillary prices and lower environmental credit sales (page:26). The Alberta average spot price was 32 per MWh over nine months against 44 (page:34), while the realized merchant price was 104 against 107, which shows the hedging programme absorbed most of the price fall (page:34). The source gives a sensitivity of about 1 million of Adjusted EBITDA per 1 per MWh change in Alberta spot for the rest of 2026, and hedged production of 6,732 GWh at 65 per MWh for full-year 2027 (page:24). Credit implication (analyst interpretation): on the hedge volumes reported, earnings are more resilient to Alberta price weakness than spot prices suggest through 2027, but the earnings stream lost at Centralia is not replaced, and the sources state 77 per cent of Alberta capacity is exposed to the merchant market (page:12).

fields.value: Adjusted EBITDA excludes costs that are real cash costs in the period. The reconciliation excludes Centralia Order compliance costs and community fund expenses of 27 in Q3 and 38 over nine months, termination and restructuring costs of 18, legal costs of 9, ERP integration costs of 6 and acquisition-related costs of 4 over nine months (page:54, page:56). The Centralia costs relate to the U.S. Department of Energy order that keeps the unit available; FERC rejected the company's cost recovery petitions for the first and second 90-day orders on Oct. 1 and 19, 2026, while affirming the ability to recover costs and allowing new petitions (page:65). No recovery is recognised in the figures supplied. A reader who treats the Order costs as recurring while the Order is renewed (four consecutive 90-day orders so far) should deduct them: Calculations C10 shows the effect on leverage.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Operating cash flow before working capital fell to 386 from 509 over nine months, and cash flow from operating activities to 317 from 415, helped by a working capital movement that the source attributes to lower collateral provided (page:43). FCF (management-defined, after sustaining capital, preferred dividends and non-controlling interest distributions, before common dividends) was 338 against 421; common dividends paid were 59, so FCF less common dividends is 279 (Calculations C9). The cash balance rose from 205 to 345, but the cash flow statement shows 338 of net proceeds from the common share issue; without it cash would have fallen by 198 (Calculations C9). The source says the offering proceeds funded the cash portion of the Colorado acquisition and were partly used to repay the drawn syndicated facility in the interim (page:5). Credit implication (analyst interpretation): internal cash generation covered dividends and capital spending but not the acquisitions, debt repayment and Order costs without the equity raise; the Colorado cash consideration was pre-funded rather than leaving a free cushion.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: TransAlta is a listed power generator with no controlling owner disclosed in the sources, whose credit profile is set by three things: a part-contracted, part-merchant fleet, a deliberate shift away from coal toward gas and data centre demand, and a programme of acquisitions and partial asset sales that is changing where its debt sits. The fleet is diversified by fuel and region (hydro, wind and solar, gas, with Alberta, other Canadian provinces, the United States and Western Australia), and 53 per cent of capacity is contracted with a weighted average contract life of 9 years; but 61 per cent of capacity is in Alberta and 77 per cent of that is exposed to the merchant market, which the company hedges through commercial customer contracts and financial hedges (hedged production of 9,364 GWh for 2026 and 6,732 GWh for 2027). The significant business changes in the last twelve months are the end of coal-fired operation at Centralia Unit 2 (kept available under a U.S. Department of Energy order whose costs the company has not yet recovered), the retirement of the Ada cogeneration facility, the mothballing of Sheerness Unit 1, Battle River Units 4 and 5 and Sundance 6, the Far North acquisition in Ontario, and the Colorado gas acquisition and Oklahoma wind minority sale that closed on Oct. 22, 2026, after the Sept. 30 balance sheet date. Each of these moves has a different credit mechanism: contracted gas assets add visible cash flow but bring assumed project debt; a minority sale at asset level raises cash while giving a co-owner a share of the Oklahoma cash flows; mothballing preserves optionality but gives up near-term earnings and relies on data centre demand that is, in the company's words, still progressing. Management and board changes in 2026 (a new chief executive from April 30, a new chief financial officer from May 1) coincide with a large capital programme. The company's own characterisations of its position are management language and are labelled so; the documented actions suggest funding discipline (equity issued ahead of the acquisition, credit facility repaid, facility maturities extended) but the pack gives no covenants, debt documents or ownership detail from which creditor protections could be assessed.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Colorado acquisition (subsequent event, closed Oct. 22, 2026). The company acquired Mountain Peak Power and Canyon Peak Power, two fully contracted natural gas-fired peaking facilities totalling 318 MW near Denver, from an indirect subsidiary of Blackstone, Inc. The purchase price was US$1 billion, including the assumption of US$750 million of project debt; the US$250 million cash portion was funded by the common share offering completed on June 9, 2026 (18,230,000 shares at 19.20 per share, gross proceeds of about 350). The agreement was announced on June 3, 2026 and was subject to Canyon Peak Power reaching commercial in-service and regulatory approvals; closing came on Oct. 22, 2026 (Q2 release page:4 and page:5; Q3 release page:5 and page:98). The accounting is a business combination whose fair values and purchase price allocation are not yet determined (Q3 release page:98). Credit mechanism: the group takes on US$750 million of project-level debt that is not on the Sept. 30 balance sheet, backed by contracted peaking assets, while the cash cost was pre-funded with equity. The sources give no EBITDA, debt terms, amortization or covenants for the assumed project debt, so its effect on consolidated leverage is not calculable and its ranking against group creditors is Insufficient Information.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Oklahoma wind minority sale (subsequent event, completed Oct. 22, 2026). The company sold a 49 per cent interest in its 500 MW Oklahoma wind portfolio (White Rock West, White Rock East, Horizon Hill) to Ares Infrastructure funds for cash proceeds of US$305 million before closing adjustments, and keeps operational oversight under a long-term asset management agreement (Q3 release page:5, page:98). Credit mechanism: cash comes in and the company keeps control and an operating role, but a co-owner now takes 49 per cent of the portfolio's cash flows, giving an outside investor 49 per cent of the portfolio; the accounting treatment, the EBITDA given up and the use of proceeds are not supplied. Management describes the transaction as "strengthening our balance sheet" (Management Language, Q3 release page:2); that effect is not quantified in the pack.

Four natural gas-fired facilities totalling 310 MW in Ontario for a purchase price of 95 subject to adjustments (aggregate 107 including working capital adjustments of 12), funded from cash and credit facility borrowings (Q1 release page:4; Q3 release page:77). The acquired business contributed revenue of 27 and earnings before taxes of 4 from Feb. 2 to Sept. 30, 2026 (Q3 release page:77).

Net proceeds of 338 are in the nine-month cash flow statement (Q3 release page:70).

fields.value: Module CP-2 (fundamental credit synthesis) for TRANSALTA CORP (issuer id tac, TransAlta Corporation and subsidiaries, consolidated), as of 2026-11-05, cutoff 2026-11-05. Pathway credit_snapshot. Reporting currency CAD, current period Q3 2026, prior period FY2025. This module synthesises the settled financial base handoff and the business and transaction handoff; it adds no source evidence of its own and re-reads the filings only to confirm that the upstream figures it uses are stated there. It contains no peer ranking, no instrument recommendation and no recovery conclusion. Ratings are quoted as the issuer reports them. Every figure below is taken from the financial base handoff unless a line says it is calculated here.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The synthesis rests on the two upstream handoffs, which rest on these sources; figures used here were also confirmed against the Q3 release.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: TransAlta's fundamental credit position is that of a diversified, partly contracted power generator with strong stated liquidity and a visible hedge programme, whose leverage has drifted above management's own target range as the earnings base narrowed, and whose portfolio is being reshaped by transactions that closed after the balance sheet date. On the financial side, management's Adjusted Net Debt to Adjusted EBITDA is 4.1 times at Sept. 30, 2026 against 4.0 times at Dec. 31, 2025, with the calculated balance-sheet ratios at 4.19 times total debt and 3.85 times net debt (financial base handoff, Chart data: leverage); the rise comes from last-four-quarter Adjusted EBITDA of 1,006 against 1,104, because Total Consolidated Net Debt fell to 3,450 from 3,725. Cover is adequate but lower: Adjusted EBITDA to cash interest paid is 3.80 times for nine months 2026 against 4.18 times for nine months 2025. Liquidity is the principal support: 1,867 of Available liquidity, no cash drawn on 2,222 of committed facilities, a syndicated facility maturing in Q2 2030 and bilateral facilities in Q2 2028, and long-term debt maturities of only 52 in 2026 and 332 in 2027. On the business side, 53 per cent of capacity is contracted with a nine-year weighted average life, hedges cover 9,364 GWh for 2026 and 6,732 GWh for 2027 at about 65 per MWh, and the fleet spans hydro, wind and solar and gas across four regions; but 61 per cent of capacity is in Alberta with 77 per cent exposed to the merchant market, the coal earnings at Centralia have ended, and thermal units (Sheerness Unit 1, Battle River Units 4 and 5 and Sundance 6) are mothballed or being mothballed with an earnings effect that is not quantified. The main creditor-relevant uncertainty is structural: 1,585 of non-recourse and OCP bond debt sits behind distribution tests, one project entity failed its Q3 test, US$750 million of project debt was assumed on Oct. 22, 2026 with no terms in the sources, and the instrument-level ranking, guarantees and covenants of the group debt are not supplied. This is a Medium-confidence view: liquidity and near-term maturity facts are well supported by filed statements, while leverage direction, forward earnings and structural ranking rest on management-defined measures and incomplete documents. Issuer-reported ratings of BB+ (S&P, outlook negative) and Ba1 (Moody's, stable) are consistent with a sub-investment-grade profile and are context only.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: First, leverage is above management's target and has moved the wrong way for a reason that is earnings, not debt: the financial base handoff shows Total Consolidated Net Debt down from 3,725 to 3,450 and credit facility drawings repaid from 95 to nil, yet last-four-quarter Adjusted EBITDA fell from 1,104 to 1,006, lifting the reported ratio from 4.0 times to 4.1 times. The fall in nine-month Adjusted EBITDA (759 against 857) is more than explained by Energy Transition (down 90, the end of coal at Centralia) and Hydro (down 48, lower Alberta prices and credit sales), while Gas improved by 32 and the third quarter was up 26. The Centralia loss is permanent in the sources' terms; the Hydro fall depends on Alberta prices. Creditors should read the 4.1 times as a ratio whose denominator has not yet stabilised.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Second, liquidity and near-term maturities are comfortable on reported figures: 1,867 of Available liquidity against long-term debt maturing of 550 across 2026 to 2028 (calculated below, about 3.39 times), no cash drawings, and facility extensions to 2030 and 2028. Two qualifications apply: 211 of non-committed letters of credit reduce committed availability, and some cash is held in project entities (the sources give 100 and 84 for restricted cash and do not reconcile them), so the freely movable share of the 345 of cash is not calculable.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Third, the cash generation base is weaker than the earnings headline suggests. Operating cash flow was 317 against 415, free cash flow 338 against 421, and the nine-month cash increase of 140 would have been a decrease of 198 without 338 of share proceeds, which were raised mainly to pre-fund the Colorado cash price. Free cash flow still covered common dividends of 59 with 279 to spare, so distributions are not the pressure point; acquisitions, debt repayment and the Centralia Order costs are.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fourth, the October 2026 transactions shift the debt profile in ways the Sept. 30 statements do not show. The Colorado acquisition adds US$750 million of assumed project debt and contracted peaking capacity of 318 MW; the Oklahoma sale brings in US$305 million of cash and gives an outside investor 49 per cent of that wind portfolio. The sources supply neither the acquired earnings nor the debt terms, so the direction of net leverage cannot be determined from the pack.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fifth, the Centralia Order imposes costs that are real cash costs and excluded from Adjusted EBITDA (38 over nine months, 27 in Q3). The unit's coal-fired operations ended but a federal order keeps it available in 90-day steps, and FERC rejected the first two cost recovery petitions while allowing new ones. If the Order continues without recovery, deducting the nine-month cost lifts the illustrative leverage figures to 4.36 times total debt and 4.00 times net debt (financial base handoff, Calculations C10, which excludes any pre-2026 Order cost).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths. Liquidity: 1,867 of Available liquidity, no cash drawn on 2,222 of committed facilities, extended maturities, and small debt maturities in 2026 (52) and 2027 (332). Revenue visibility: 53 per cent of capacity is contracted with a weighted average life of 9 years, and hedged production is 9,364 GWh for 2026 and 6,732 GWh for 2027, which the sources show absorbed most of the 2026 fall in Alberta spot prices (realized merchant price 104 against 107 while spot fell to 32 from 44). Diversification: 89 facilities in four regions across hydro, wind and solar and gas. Balance sheet repair in absolute terms: drawn credit facilities repaid, Total Consolidated Net Debt down by 275, interest expense down to 241 from 266 over nine months. Contracted growth: Far North and Colorado add contracted gas capacity, and the Centralia conversion has a tolling agreement with capacity payments through 2044. Prudent pre-funding: the Colorado cash price was equity funded before closing.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Weaknesses. Leverage above target at 4.1 times with the calculated total and net ratios at 4.19 and 3.85 times, and rising since December. Narrowed earnings base: nine-month Adjusted EBITDA down 98, with a lost coal earnings stream and unquantified effects from the mothballed thermal units (Sheerness Unit 1, Battle River Units 4 and 5, Sundance 6). Alberta concentration: 61 per cent of capacity and 77 per cent merchant exposure, with hedge cover that the sources document only to 2027. Structural opacity: 1,585 of non-recourse and OCP debt behind distribution tests (one entity failed its test), exchangeable securities of 750 classified as current, US$750 million of assumed project debt, and no guarantee or ranking detail for 1,673 of senior unsecured debt. Cash flow softness: operating cash flow 317 against 415 and free cash flow 338 against 421, and a nine-month cash build dependent on share proceeds. Unrecovered Order costs and a negative outlook at one rating agency, with up to 59 of credit-contingent collateral. Reliance on management-defined measures for EBITDA, net debt and free cash flow, none of which can be tied to covenant definitions from the pack.

fields.value: Module CP-5 (evidence trace validation with the research-integrity grade) for TRANSALTA CORP (issuer id tac, TransAlta Corporation and subsidiaries), as of 2026-11-05, cutoff 2026-11-05. Pathway credit_snapshot, reporting currency CAD, current period Q3 2026, prior period FY2025. The reader question is whether the analysis is traceable enough for a committee decision and which provenance gap matters most. Scope is the Top 5 credit drivers plus every figure that two or more handoffs share. The review is independent of the author: each driver was re-opened in the retained Q3 release, and the key ratios were recomputed from the printed inputs. It changes no upstream conclusion and repairs no lineage silently; where a handoff is wrong or overstated, the defect is logged and the earlier handoff stays as accepted. No numeric confidence score is computed here because the scoring script is not part of this transport; the QA status and committee status are stated with reasons.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Committee use is restricted. The financial base is well traced: sampled figures in the earnings, balance sheet, cash flow, debt, facility and maturity tables agree with the Q3 release, the ratios recompute from printed inputs, and the figures shared across the three analytical handoffs are identical. Traceability weakens where the analysis moves from facts to mechanisms about structure: the Oklahoma control statement, the description of the assumed Colorado debt as asset-backed, and the contracted status of Far North in the synthesis lack a source in the handoffs that make them. Those are bounded defects, none changes the leverage, liquidity or earnings conclusions, and each has a stated fix. The most material provenance gap is absence of covenant, indenture and transaction documents, which limits structural conclusions however carefully the figures are traced.
